title: Don't Throw Away Your Beams: Improving Consistency-based Uncertainties in LLMs via Beam Search
claim: Random sampling yields duplicate answers and a noisy confidence estimate, while beam search covers distinct top answers for a better score.
layout: Top chat prompt, then 2 side-by-side boxed panels with ✗/✓ marks
description: The top shows a chat scenario. A user icon asks 'Who sang the song Thriller in 20th century?'. A robot icon replies 'Michael Jackson' with a green check. A thought bubble from a second user icon asks 'How confident is this answer?'. Below are two boxed panels. The left panel, 'Multinomial Sampling', shows a robot icon with five yellow or blue answer bubbles: Prince (red ✗) three times and Michael Jackson (green ✓) twice. Its confidence reads '2 / 5' in dark red. The right panel, 'Beam Search Decoding', shows five distinct color-coded answers, each with a probability: Michael Jackson 0.39 ✓, Prince 0.34 ✗, M. Jackson 0.19 ✓, Bruno Mars 0.05 ✗, Kai Angel 0.03 ✗. Its confidence reads '0.58' in green. The eye goes first to the question, then to the contrasting panels and confidence values.
caption: Beam Search vs Multinomial Sampling. Sampling produces multiple identical generations resulting in noisy confidence estimate, while beam search covers top answers from LLM distribution resulting in a better confidence score.
abstract: Consistency-based methods have emerged as an effective approach to uncertainty quantification (UQ) in large language models. These methods typically rely on several generations obtained via multinomial sampling, measuring their agreement level. However, in short-form QA, multinomial sampling is prone to producing duplicates due to peaked distributions, and its stochasticity introduces considerable variance in uncertainty estimates across runs. We introduce a new family of methods that employ beam search to generate candidates for consistency-based UQ, yielding improved performance and reduced variance compared to multinomial sampling. We also provide a theoretical lower bound on the beam set probability mass under which beam search achieves a smaller error than multinomial sampling. We empirically evaluate our approach on six QA datasets and find that its consistent improvements over multinomial sampling lead to state-of-the-art UQ performance.
